source.title: Explicit Regularization via Regularizer Mirror Descent
source.authors: Navid Azizan; Sahin Lale; B. Hassibi

page_placements.theme: Modified training can suppress or reverse corrupted-target fitting

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation that affects the cataloged results.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own ResNet-18 experiments on corrupted labels, showing SGD fits them while RMD and weight decay often do not; these results refine the scope of random-label fitting and regularization claims.
record.gate_note: The paper reports experiments with label-corruption fractions, including random label assignment, and compares training and test accuracy for SGD, RMD, and weight decay. It does not test shuffled pixels, Gaussian-noise inputs, smooth test-error degradation across corruption levels for a single training method, explicit regularizers on random labels, or learning order over training. Mentioned prior-work results are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The SGD controls directly test interpolation and test accuracy as random-label corruption increases, bearing on V4. Weight-decay experiments and the clean-data SGD control also bear on V5. The proposed RMD method's performance is not itself a test of standard SGD fitting random labels.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase broadly matches the authors' conclusion: RMD provides robust generalization under label corruption and generally outperforms SGD and weight decay. Qualify the empirical comparison: improvement over SGD is small at 10% corruption, and SGD performs best on clean data. RMD's convergence guarantees require stated assumptions.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates a new regularizer mirror descent algorithm against mini-batch SGD and weight decay on ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 with partially corrupted labels; it does not reproduce the original fully randomized-label experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Corruption fraction and regularization parameter λ change training and test accuracies; the authors report weight decay test accuracy as erratic and sensitive to λ, while RMD test accuracy is comparatively stable.

fits_no_version.finding: RMD trades training fit against generalization through a deliberately regularized objective, with performance varying across λ and corruption levels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RMD can improve generalization on partially label-corrupted CIFAR-10 while avoiding interpolation of the original training labels.

record.problems: The experiments cover only ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 and partial label corruption, with no completely random-label condition. Reported results use the best-performing learning rate choices; the text does not report uncertainty estimates or repeated-run statistics, though it notes that different weight-decay runs with the same hyperparameters can have drastically different test accuracies.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. The paper also reports uncorrupted-label results, but those do not bear on the tested versions concerning random labels or label noise.

untested.parts: Completely random training labels, chance-level test performance, and unchanged hyperparameters relative to a fully randomized condition.
Training-time ratios and convergence slowdown as corruption increases; no timing or learning-curve comparison is reported.
All shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, and Gaussian-input conditions.
Corruption above 40%, the fully random endpoint, and convergence of test accuracy to chance. Aggregate accuracies do not separately measure learning signal and memorizing noise.
Fully randomized datasets; dropout; augmentation ablations; removal of all explicit regularization. The clean SGD condition retains fixed crop-and-flip augmentation.
Learning order of real versus noisy labels; only final accuracies are reported.

missing.what: Clean-data SGD control: 100% training accuracy and 92.81% test accuracy without weight decay, with fixed augmentation. The record declares clean results excluded, but its rationale incorrectly dismisses their relevance to V5; restore this control for the text-based verdict.
missing.versions: V5; also supplies V4's zero-corruption baseline

record.verdict_notes: Randomization fractions of 10%, 25%, and 40% imply approximately 9%, 22.5%, and 36% actually incorrect labels. SGD was explicitly trained until 100% training accuracy; regularized methods used convergence criteria over 500 consecutive epochs. Learning rates were selected separately by algorithm. Fixed augmentation was retained. Missing endpoints are untested, not evidence against V4.

versions.untested_parts: Tests random-label corruption only as part of 10%, 25%, and 40% dataset corruption; does not test a completely random labeling of the entire training set or test error at chance.
Reports separate corruption levels and metrics, but does not test the claim that training accuracy stays perfect while test error rises steadily toward chance for one method.
Does not test weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation on a completely random labeling, nor whether removing these methods alone harms true-label generalization.
